story_text.value:
I'm a bit nostalgic. There are some podcasts I started listening to years ago (2017~), but not at the start (2008~). At a certain point, the podcast changes, maybe some stalwarts rotate out of the main line-up... I just want to go back, to the beginning.

I'm also someone that has no self-restraint. I'll mainline ten of the same podcast in a day, then forget all about listening to no.11. Podcasts apps do not help this: It's hard to get them to cooperate in a way which surfaces your next episode in the 'Latest episodes' list, because while it may be up next for you, it was actually released 15 years ago.

PodcastDelay solves that, by taking that original feed and 'delaying' it by however long you want. It's a solution for re-publishing a podcast's RSS feed as a new private feed. It can start releasing from any episode, at any cadence, including mirroring the original release cadence.

If a show has two feeds — the regular one and a premium/bonus one — you can merge them into a single delayed feed. Each bonus episode comes out the same distance after its free counterpart as it did originally: an hour stays an hour, a day stays a day, whatever cadence you're replaying the free feed at.

Audio isn't hosted/reposted, but there are plenty of solutions if you wanted to have 'local' media turned into an RSS feed, which PodcastDelay could then put out in the correct cadence.

title.value: Show HN: PodcastDelay – an open source RSS feed generator

story_text.value:
I have been playing with a lot of $20 devices with no keyboards or screens. I wanted to use speech to interact with them, but without it having to run through a cloud service or use a fixed command vocabulary.

I worked with Claude to implement high performance 4bit int kernels for the ESP32S3 and P4 and quantize some larger STT and TTS models. Surprisingly, it's quite usable on these tiny boards.

Also includes a finetuned model that can better cope with my diesel drones, hacking coughs, and mumbling. Works with Micropython (RAM scarcity issues) and AtomVM (better).

title.value: Show HN: Babytalk: Offline speech to text and text to speech on ESP32

story_text.value:
Talus is a small diffusion model that makes game heightmaps and runs entirely in the browser.

try it at: https://talus.tersa.tech

It has 23M parameters and it was trained from scratch. The training data was 45K maps from my own generator.

I made it to get terrain I can ask for whenever. The best part is that it can run on a consumer GPU (For e.g. I trained it on an RTX 5060).

It's limits are the 64x64 maps, and it was only trained on procedural maps.

The GitHub link is: https://github.com/osfv/talus It's fully open source with the Apache License!

What do you think i could improve on the model?

title.value: Show HN: Talus, a small terrain diffusion model that runs in the browser

story_text.value:
This past week I built (prompted) a tool I find myself using day to day and wanted to share it with others who may find it useful as well.

“Lacuna” is an opinionated way to invoke LLMs into any text input on your Mac. Specifically, you can type bracketed phrases {such as this}, press Shift-Command-K (or a different shortcut of your choosing), and the tool sends your bracketed phrase + the surrounding text contents to an LLM of your configuration for generating text to replace the bracketed phrase. The program returns 3 candidate phrases and the experience is entirely keyboard navigable.

Demo: https://jackdamon.org/assets/images/lacuna-scheduling-demo.g...

Example scheduling workflow using Lacuna’s native UI and sample suggestions.

So far I find myself frequently using it when drafting emails where I want help with quick phrasing.

The project was inspired by Rectangle, an open source utility app for window tiling that is keyboard based.

Lacuna is open source and available here: https://github.com/jdamon96/lacuna

Blog: https://jackdamon.org/blog/lacuna/

title.value: Show HN: Lacuna – open-source inline AI writing suggestions for your Mac

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I built this after watching long Claude Code sessions fill up with tool output: a single verbose test run or build log can be 30–50k characters, almost all of it PASSED lines, warnings and lockfile churn. The context fills, compaction comes sooner, and the agent forgets earlier instructions.

Context Diet is a mod (Claude Code's new JS hook API) that rewrites tool results before they are stored in the conversation:

- test runners and build tools (jest, vitest, pytest, go test, cargo, tsc, eslint, npm/pip install, docker build) get parsed digests: every failure with its message and location, plus the summary; passing tests are counted, not listed - JSON becomes a skeleton, diffs drop lockfile churn, grep results and file lists are grouped, tables keep exact first and last rows - running the same command again shows only what changed - the full output is always saved to a file, and the digest says where, so the agent can read it when it needs more

The question I cared about most was whether it makes the agent worse. On 7 Q&A tasks with known answers, both groups were 7/7, with 8 tool calls instead of 13. On a bug-fixing task (600 tests, two hidden bugs, Haiku/Sonnet/Opus, 18 runs) every agent fixed both bugs with or without it, using 6 tool calls instead of 8.

Honest caveats: the token saving on very large outputs is modest, because Claude Code already moves those to a file; the gain there is fewer steps. Also, when a command fails, Claude Code keeps only ~10k characters and drops the end of the output, where the failures usually are. There is an opt-in mode that saves the whole output first, off by default because it changes the command text.

It's MIT, makes no network calls, and I'd love examples of output it digests badly.

title.value: Show HN: Context Diet – trims tool output before it floods Claude Code's context
